title: Relations and Their Properties
short: A relation on A is a set of ordered pairs; check whether it is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive.
trouble: Students think "antisymmetric" means "not symmetric." Equality is both, and some relations are neither.

blocks.html: "Is less than," "divides," "is a sibling of," "has the same remainder as": each of these relates some pairs of things and not others. Using Cartesian products, a relation becomes a set of ordered pairs, and four properties sort relations into the families that matter most.

A relation $R$ on a set $A$ is a subset of $A \times A$; we write $a\,R\,b$ when $(a, b) \in R$. $R$ is reflexive if $a\,R\,a$ for every $a \in A$; symmetric if $a\,R\,b$ implies $b\,R\,a$; antisymmetric if $a\,R\,b$ and $b\,R\,a$ together imply $a = b$; transitive if $a\,R\,b$ and $b\,R\,c$ imply $a\,R\,c$.

Each property is easy to see in a picture where every pair $(a, b)$ is an arrow from $a$ to $b$. Reflexive: a loop at every point (in the matrix, $1$'s all down the diagonal). Symmetric: every arrow has a return arrow (the matrix equals its transpose). Antisymmetric: no two different points have arrows both ways. Transitive: every two-step route $a \to b \to c$ has the shortcut $a \to c$. Each property is a "for all" statement, so one missing pair is enough to break it.

blocks.title: Checking all four properties
steps: Symmetric: the only non-loop pairs are $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$, each the reverse of the other. Yes.
Transitive: check every route. $1 \to 2 \to 1$ needs $(1, 1)$: present. $2 \to 1 \to 2$ needs $(2, 2)$: present. Every other route uses a loop. Yes.
blocks.a: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive; not antisymmetric

blocks.title: "Divides" on a small set
blocks.q: On $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, let $a\,R\,b$ mean $a \mid b$. Which properties hold?
steps: Antisymmetric: if $a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$ for positive integers, then $a \le b$ and $b \le a$, so $a = b$. Yes.
Transitive: $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$ give $a \mid c$ (proved in the direct-proof lesson). Yes.

blocks.title: Counting relations
blocks.q: How many relations are there on a set with $3$ elements?
steps: A relation is any subset of $A \times A$, which has $3 \cdot 3 = 9$ pairs.
Each pair is in or out: $2^{9} = 512$ relations.

blocks.html: Reading "antisymmetric" as "not symmetric." They are different ideas. Equality is both symmetric and antisymmetric. The relation $\{(1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3)\}$ is neither: $(2, 3)$ has no return arrow, and $1$ and $2$ point at each other. Check: antisymmetric only forbids two-way arrows between different points; it says nothing about one-way arrows or loops.
